title: Phones Are Not a Symptom of Disengagement, They’re a Direct Cause of It t-cause-of-it
author: Carl Hendrick
summary: Hendrick attacks a claim circulating in education discourse that classroom phone use is a symptom of disengagement rather than a cause of it, and traces its lineage to advice he received as a new teacher in 2006. That earlier advice held that misbehaviour was evidence of insufficiently relevant planning, and in his case took the form of a suggestion that he teach Hamlet through Eminem lyrics because Shakespeare's language could not appeal to students of colour in an inner-city school. He argues the symptom framing is damaging on two fronts: it makes the teacher solely responsible for student conduct, and it patronises students by implying they can only learn if they are tricked into it. Against advocates of classroom phone use, he marshals the evidence on phones as a drag on learning and on adolescent mental health, characterising in-classroom advocacy as naive at best and a dereliction of duty at worst. The piece closes with the blunt causal assertion of its title, describing the phone as an algorithmically funded distraction machine calibrated to capture developing attention.
points: Hendrick identifies the symptom framing as a rebranding of the older orthodoxy that misbehaviour indicates a badly planned lesson, which relocates responsibility for conduct onto the teacher alone.
His account of being told to teach Hamlet through Eminem lyrics is deployed as evidence that relevance-chasing carries a condescending assumption about which students can access difficult material.
The second line of attack is that the symptom claim patronises pupils, implying they cannot learn anything unless they are, in his phrase, conned into it.
He treats the harms as double, both to learning in the classroom and to adolescent mental health more broadly, and uses that to argue phones have no legitimate classroom role.
The characterisation of the phone as a billion-dollar-funded distraction device frames the classroom contest as one against deliberate engineering rather than against pupil boredom.
quotes: One of the most damaging things I heard in my first few years of teaching was the notion that if kids were misbehaving in a lesson then it was the teacher’s fault as they hadn’t planned the lesson to properly engage them.

More specifically, I was advised to use the lyrics of Eminem to teach Hamlet because the language of Shakespeare couldn’t possibly appeal to the students of colour in the inner city school I was working in at the time.

This week I noticed this trope emerge again but this time with the added garnish of cell/mobile phone use and the risible claim that phones are not the cause of disengagement but rather a symptom of it.

This pernicious idea is damaging on two fronts: firstly it drastically undermines the extent to which a classroom teacher can do their job by placing the blame for misbehaviour squarely on their shoulders not the students and secondly it’s patronises every student in that classroom by suggesting they can’t possibly learn something unless they’re conned into it.
There is now clear evidence that phones are not just damaging for learning but they are having a catastrophic impact on teenager’s mental health and wellbeing.
Phones are arguably now the single most damaging factor for learning in the contemporary classroom and have no place in it.
The chaos machine in every students’ pocket is a thermobaric weapon of distraction fuelled by billion dollar algorithms, all carefully calibrated to steal the attention of developing young minds.
